The Nida Model 280 Rotating Trainer is a very versatile piece of equipment.
DISCUSSION
It can be configured as an AC motor, DC motor, Stepper motor, and a generator.
In order to utilize the trainer, it is important to have a firm understanding of all controls, connectors and indicators.
The controls, indicators and connectors are contained on two panels of the trainer: The Motor Control Panel and the Mimic Bus Panel.
The Motor Control Panel contains the motors, shaft couplers, electric brake, magnetic pickup assembly and 130 interface connectors.
The Mimic Bus Panel contains test points to monitor motor action and switches to control circuit setup and configuration.
Let's examine the components and connectors located on the Motor Control Panel.
There are three motors mounted on the Motor Control Panel..
The Stepper Motor is a four phase, permanent magnet rotor type.
The Stepper Motor is capable of producing 40 oz-inches of torque at full phase current (1 amp max. 1 phase).
The AC motor is a 115 VAC, 50-60 Hz split-phase, capacitor-run motor.
The AC motor is capable of producing approximately 1/50 HP at full line voltage.
The DC motor is a 24 VDC, compound wound motor.
The DC motor is capable of producing 20 oz-inches of usable torque at full rate voltage.
The Stepper gear is a 24 pitch, 60 tooth gear.
The stepper gear produces a 1 Hz frequency with a 1 RPM motor speed. This enables calculations to be performed easily.
A magnetic pickup on the stepper gear is a standard sensor.
This sensor produces speed feedback to the 130 Test Console based interface cards.
The dynamic brake consists of a fixed mount coil assembly aligned with a rotating magnetic pad coupled to the motor shaft.
The dynamic brake allows loaded and unloaded motor data to be taken in various experiments.
The shaft couplers connect the motor shafts of the stepper, AC and DC motors.
These couplers allow for slight inaccuracies in alignment without binding and loading the motors.
The guard shield is a clear plastic protector that covers all rotating components.
When operating the trainer, the guard shield should always be in place.

The next panel we will discuss is the Mimic Bus Panel......
The Mimic Bus Panel contains all the test points, configuration switches and motor control switches.
This bus panel consists of three primary sub-panels.
The stepper motor sub-panel contains test points to monitor the stepper motor.
The AC motor sub-panel contains test points and motor control switches for the AC motor.
The DC motor sub-panel contains test points and motor control switches for the DC motor.
The Stepper motor sub-panel is used when the trainer is configured for the Stepper motor.
The Stepper motor sub-panel contains six test points to monitor the individual stator winding voltages of the stepper motor.
The AC motor sub-panel is used when the trainer is configured for the AC motor.
This panel contains various test points for monitoring voltage and current in the Run and or Start windings of the AC motor.
The AC motor RUN switch applies line voltage to the run winding of the AC motor.
The AC motor Start switch applies line voltage to the start windings of the AC motor.
The AC motor Run Phase switch reverses the phase of the line voltage applied to the run winding of the AC motor.
By reversing the phase of the line voltage applied to the Run winding, the AC motor output shaft will reverse its direction of rotation.
The AC motor Start phase switch reverses the phase of the applied line voltage to the start winding.
By reversing the phase of the line voltage applied to the start winding, the AC motor output shaft also reverses its direction of rotation.
If both phase switches are changed simultaneously, the direction of the output shaft rotation will not change.
The AC motor Run meter switch breaks the current path to the run windings when placed to the IN position.
This allows an ammeter to be connected for current measurements of the AC motor run windings.
The AC motor START meter switch breaks the current path to the start windings when placed to the IN position.
This allows an ammeter to be connected for current measurements of the AC motor start windings.
The AC motor line meter switch breaks current to both the start and run windings for total current measurements.
The DC motor sub-panel is used when the trainer is configured for the DC motor.
This panel contains various switches, test points and potentiometers for DC motor measurements.
The OPER/TEST switch selects between the + Power Supply voltage of the 130 or pins E and F on PC130-280 as the source.
Pins E and F receive signal voltages from the output pins of the experiment cards on the 130 Trainer.
The RUN/STOP switch selects between the source voltage and the brake load that is used to stop the motor.
In the Run position, source voltage is applied to the motor.
In the Stop position, the brake load is applied to the motor.
When the ARM/VAR switch is in the ARM position, it selects the source voltage for the shunt field.
Recall the OPER/TEST switch is used to select the type of voltage source.
When placed in the Off position, the source is removed from the shunt field winding of the DC motor.
When set in the IN position, the meter switch breaks the current path to series field winding. This allows the insertion of an ammeter..
The DC motor Shunt Field switch reverses the polarity of the shunt field winding.
The Series Field switch allows the series field winding to be (IN) the current path.
IN corresponds to the switch being open. OUT corresponds to the switch being closed.
The Dynamic Brake switch applies the (-) Supply Voltage from the 130 trainer to the Dynamic Brake circuit.
The DC Rotor switch changes the polarity of the DC rotor. This reverses the direction of shaft rotation.
After power is removed from the motor, the Brake Load potentiometer varies the load resistance applied to the motor.
The Field Current pot. varies current supplied by the (-) Supply of the 130 trainer to the shunt field winding..
The DC motor Dynamic Brake potentiometer varies the amount of Dynamic Brake applied to the motors.
This allows various loads to be applied to the motors during operation.
